decks.title: Chemical Coordination in Plants — Part 1: Plant growth regulators
goals: State one effect of each of auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid and ethylene
Distinguish growth promoters from growth inhibitors
Interpret simple experiments with plant hormones

slides.heading: Chemical Coordination in Plants
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how plants use chemical messengers to control growth.

visual.alt: Flow: a hormone is made in one part of the plant, moves to another part and causes a growth response

slides.narration: Plants have no nerves and no brain, yet they grow towards light, make fruits ripen and drop their leaves at the right time. They do all this with chemical messengers. In this part we meet the five main plant growth regulators.

slides.heading: Plant growth regulators
slides.body_md: **Plant growth regulators** (phytohormones) are chemicals made in small amounts in one part of a plant that control growth and development elsewhere.

visual.alt: Table: auxin, gibberellin and cytokinin are growth promoters; abscisic acid and ethylene are growth inhibitors

slides.narration: Three of these chemicals speed up growth. They are the promoters: auxin, gibberellin and cytokinin. Two of them slow growth or bring a stage of life to an end. They are the inhibitors: abscisic acid and ethylene.

slides.heading: Where the regulators act
slides.body_md: Each regulator has typical sites and effects in the plant body.

visual.alt: Where the five plant growth regulators act in a plant

slides.narration: Auxin is made at the shoot tip. Gibberellin lengthens the stem between the leaves. Cytokinin is made in the root tips. Abscisic acid acts on leaves in dry weather, and a ripening fruit gives off ethylene.

slides.heading: Auxins

rows: Side buds stay dormant while the tip is present
Seedless fruits; less early fruit drop

visual.alt: Table of five effects of auxins with examples

slides.narration: Auxins are made at the shoot tip and move downwards. They make cells just behind the tip grow longer. They keep the side buds dormant, which we call apical dominance. Gardeners also use them to root cuttings and to grow seedless fruits.

slides.heading: Quick check: the shoot tip hormone
slides.body_md: Fill in: the hormone made at the shoot tip that stops the lateral buds from growing is ______.
slides.narration: Think of what happens when a gardener pinches off a shoot tip.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: rooting cuttings
slides.body_md: A nursery plants 40 rose cuttings dipped in rooting powder and 40 untreated ones.
bullets: Step 1: rooted cuttings: treated **34**, untreated **10**.
Step 2: percentage rooted: treated **85%**, untreated **25%**.
Step 3: conclusion: the **auxin** in the powder makes many more cuttings form roots.

visual.alt: Worked table: thirty-four of forty treated cuttings rooted, eighty-five percent; ten of forty untreated cuttings rooted, twenty-five percent

slides.narration: Always compare a treated set with a control. Here most treated cuttings rooted, but only a quarter of the untreated ones did. The difference is the effect of the auxin. The few untreated cuttings that rooted used their own natural auxin.

slides.heading: Gibberellins and cytokinins

rows: Lengthen internodes; dwarf plants grow tall
Break dormancy of seeds and buds
Delay ageing: leaves stay green longer
Bolting of rosette plants such as cabbage
Rich in coconut water; made in root tips

visual.alt: Table comparing the effects of gibberellins and cytokinins

slides.narration: Gibberellins make stems longer, so genetically dwarf plants can reach normal height. They also wake seeds from dormancy. Cytokinins make cells divide and keep leaves green for longer. Coconut water is a natural source of cytokinins.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: dwarf peas
slides.body_md: Dwarf pea seedlings were sprayed with water or with gibberellin.
bullets: Step 1: mean heights after three weeks: water **12 cm**, gibberellin **30 cm**.
Step 2: difference: 30 − 12 = **18 cm**.
Step 3: ratio: 30 ÷ 12 = **2.5** times taller.

visual.alt: Worked table: seedlings sprayed with water grew to twelve centimetres; seedlings sprayed with gibberellin grew to thirty centimetres

slides.narration: Gibberellin made the dwarf seedlings two and a half times taller than the control. The extra growth comes from longer internodes, not from more leaves. This is how gibberellin overcomes genetic dwarfism.

slides.heading: Quick check: green leaves
slides.body_md: Which hormone promotes cell division and delays the ageing of leaves?
slides.narration: This hormone is plentiful in coconut water.

slides.heading: Abscisic acid and ethylene

rows: Closes stomata when water is short: the stress hormone
Hastens yellowing and ageing of leaves
Promotes the fall of leaves and fruits
Promotes the fall of leaves, flowers and fruits

visual.alt: Table comparing the effects of abscisic acid and ethylene

slides.narration: Abscisic acid helps a plant survive hard times. It shuts the stomata in a drought and keeps seeds dormant until conditions improve. Ethylene is a gas. It ripens fruits, and one ripe fruit can ripen a whole box of raw ones.

slides.heading: Quick check: a gaseous hormone
slides.body_md: Which plant growth regulator is a gas at ordinary temperatures?
slides.narration: It is the hormone of fruit ripening.

slides.heading: Promoters and inhibitors work together

visual.alt: Table of three processes, the hormone that promotes each and the hormone that opposes it

slides.narration: A plant rarely uses one hormone alone. Gibberellin and abscisic acid pull in opposite directions over germination. Auxin and cytokinin balance each other over side buds. The final growth depends on the balance between them.

slides.heading: Quick check: longer internodes
slides.body_md: True or false: gibberellins cause the internodes of a stem to lengthen.
slides.narration: Remember the dwarf peas.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Auxin: cell elongation, apical dominance, rooting, seedless fruits, weedicides.
Gibberellin: longer internodes, breaks dormancy, bolting, larger fruits.
Cytokinin: cell division, delays ageing of leaves.
Abscisic acid: closes stomata, dormancy, leaf fall.
Ethylene: a gas; ripening, ageing and leaf fall.

visual.alt: Summary table: promoters are auxin, gibberellin and cytokinin; inhibitors are abscisic acid and ethylene

slides.narration: To recap. Auxin, gibberellin and cytokinin are promoters. Abscisic acid and ethylene are inhibitors. Learn one clear effect and one everyday use for each, and you will be ready for most questions.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Give **one precise effect** for each hormone: "auxin causes apical dominance", not "auxin helps growth".
Remember **ethylene is a gas** and an **inhibitor**.
Abscisic acid is the **stress hormone**: it **closes** stomata.
In experiment questions, always name the **control** and say what it shows.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Be precise about each hormone. Ethylene is a gas and an inhibitor. Abscisic acid closes stomata, it does not open them. And in experiments, say which set is the control and why it is needed.

decks.title: Chemical Coordination in Plants — Part 2: Tropic movements
goals: Identify the type of tropism from an example and say whether it is positive or negative
Explain phototropism of a shoot in terms of unequal auxin distribution
Describe simple experiments on phototropism, geotropism and hydrotropism

slides.heading: Tropic Movements
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how plant parts grow towards or away from a stimulus.

visual.alt: Flow: a stimulus from one side causes unequal auxin, which causes unequal growth and bending

slides.narration: A plant cannot walk towards the sun, but its shoot can grow towards it. Its roots grow down into the soil and towards water. These slow, directional growth responses are called tropic movements, or tropisms.

slides.heading: Five tropisms
slides.body_md: A **tropism** is the growth of a plant part towards (**positive**) or away from (**negative**) a stimulus coming from one direction.

rows: Root grows down (positive); shoot grows up (negative)
Pollen tube grows to the ovule

visual.alt: Table of five tropisms with their stimulus and an example of each

slides.narration: Name a tropism after its stimulus: photo for light, geo for gravity, hydro for water, thigmo for touch and chemo for chemicals. Then say positive if the part grows towards the stimulus, or negative if it grows away.

slides.heading: Phototropism
slides.body_md: A shoot lit from one side **bends towards the light**: it is **positively phototropic**.

slides.heading: How auxin makes a shoot bend

nodes.label: Light falls on one side of the tip
Auxin moves to the shaded side

visual.alt: Flow: light on one side of the tip, auxin moves to the shaded side, cells there elongate more, the shoot curves towards the light

slides.narration: The tip senses the light. Auxin then moves to the shaded side and travels down. Cells on the shaded side grow longer than cells on the lit side. A stem that is longer on one side must curve towards the shorter side, which faces the light.

bullets: Step 1: what is the **stimulus**: light, gravity, water, touch or chemicals?
Step 2: does the part grow **towards** it (positive) or **away** (negative)?
Step 3: join them: for example, positive hydrotropism.

Shoot grows up in a dark cupboard

slides.heading: Worked example 2: predicting with a clinostat
slides.body_md: A **clinostat** turns a seedling slowly so that gravity acts on all sides in turn.
bullets: Step 1: seedling laid flat, **not** rotating: root curves down, shoot curves up.
Step 2: seedling laid flat **on a rotating clinostat**: both keep growing **horizontally**.
Step 3: conclusion: the curving in step 1 was caused by **gravity** acting from one side.

visual.alt: Worked table: a still seedling curves, a seedling on a rotating clinostat grows straight

slides.narration: The clinostat is the control for gravity. When the seedling turns slowly, every side faces down for the same time, so there is no one-sided pull. Without a one-sided stimulus, there is no tropism.

slides.body_md: Fill in: the instrument that slowly rotates a seedling so that gravity acts equally on all sides is a ______.
slides.narration: Its name begins like the word incline.

slides.heading: Quick check: roots and water
slides.body_md: True or false: roots show negative hydrotropism.
slides.narration: Do roots grow towards water or away from it?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: A tropism is growth towards (positive) or away from (negative) a one-sided stimulus.
Shoots: positively phototropic, negatively geotropic.
Roots: positively geotropic and hydrotropic, negatively phototropic.
Tendrils: thigmotropism. Pollen tubes: chemotropism.
Auxin on the shaded side makes those cells grow longer, so the shoot bends to light.

visual.alt: Summary table of how shoots and roots respond to light, gravity and water

slides.narration: To recap. Shoots grow towards light and away from gravity. Roots grow towards gravity and water and away from light. Tendrils respond to touch and pollen tubes to chemicals. Unequal auxin makes unequal growth, and that is what bends the plant.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Always write **positive** or **negative** with the tropism.
Auxin collects on the **shaded** side, not the lit side.
The **tip** senses light; the **region below** it bends.
For experiments, give **set-up, observation and conclusion**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Never write just phototropism: say positive or negative. Put auxin on the shaded side. Remember that the tip senses and the region below bends. And describe every experiment in three parts: set-up, observation and conclusion.

notes.title: Chemical Coordination in Plants — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Plant growth regulators
sections.body_md:
Plants have no nervous system. They coordinate growth with **plant growth regulators** (**phytohormones**): chemicals made in **small amounts** in one part of the plant that **move** to other parts and control growth and development.

| Group | Regulators | General effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Growth promoters** | Auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins | Speed up cell division, cell elongation, germination, fruit growth |
| **Growth inhibitors** | Abscisic acid (ABA), ethylene | Slow growth; bring about dormancy, ripening, ageing and leaf fall |

Hormones often act **together or against each other**: gibberellin breaks dormancy while abscisic acid maintains it; auxin from the tip suppresses side buds while cytokinin helps them grow.

key_terms.definition_md: A chemical made in small amounts in one part of a plant that controls growth elsewhere.
A regulator that speeds up growth: auxin, gibberellin, cytokinin.
A regulator that slows growth: abscisic acid, ethylene.

sections.heading: 2. Effects of each regulator
sections.body_md:
| Regulator | Main effects | Everyday use |
|---|---|---|
| **Auxin** (made at shoot tips) | Cell **elongation** just below the tip; **apical dominance** (lateral buds stay dormant); root formation; fruit growth | Rooting powder for **cuttings**; **seedless fruits**; prevents early fruit drop; synthetic **2,4-D** kills broad-leaved weeds |
| **Gibberellin** | **Lengthens internodes** (dwarf plants grow tall); breaks **dormancy** of seeds and buds; **bolting** of rosette plants | Larger grapes; faster germination of barley |
| **Cytokinin** (made in root tips; rich in coconut water) | Promotes **cell division**; **delays ageing** of leaves; helps lateral buds grow | Keeps cut leaves and flowers fresh; tissue culture |
| **Abscisic acid** — the **stress hormone** | **Closes stomata** when water is short; keeps seeds and buds **dormant**; promotes **leaf fall** | Helps crops survive drought |
| **Ethylene** — a **gas** | **Ripens fruits**; hastens **ageing** and fall of leaves, flowers and fruits | Ripening of bananas and mangoes in closed rooms |

**Apical dominance.** The shoot tip makes auxin, which moves down and keeps lateral buds dormant. Removing the tip (pinching, pruning, plucking tea) removes the auxin, so side shoots grow and the plant becomes bushy.

key_terms.definition_md: Suppression of lateral buds by auxin from the shoot tip.
Sudden lengthening of the stem of a rosette plant before flowering, caused by gibberellin.
Ageing of a leaf or other part; delayed by cytokinins.
Formation of fruit without fertilisation, giving seedless fruits.

sections.heading: 3. Tropic movements
sections.body_md:
A **tropism** (tropic movement) is the **growth** of a plant part **towards** (positive) or **away from** (negative) a **stimulus coming from one direction**. It is slow and permanent because it results from **unequal growth** on the two sides of the organ.

| Tropism | Stimulus | Positive | Negative |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Phototropism** | Light | Shoot | Root |
| **Geotropism** | Gravity | Root | Shoot |
| **Hydrotropism** | Water | Root | — |
| **Thigmotropism** | Touch / contact | Tendrils of pea, gourd, grapevine coil round a support | — |
| **Chemotropism** | Chemicals | Pollen tube grows towards the ovule | — |

The folding of *Mimosa* (touch-me-not) leaflets when touched is **not** a tropism: it is not a growth movement and does not depend on the direction of the touch.

**Experiments**
- **Geotropism:** a seedling laid flat curves its root down and its shoot up. On a slowly rotating **clinostat**, gravity acts on all sides in turn and the seedling grows straight.
- **Hydrotropism:** seeds in a tilted sieve of moist sawdust: roots grow down out of the holes, then curve back into the moist sawdust.

key_terms.definition_md: Growth movement of a plant part in response to a one-sided stimulus.
An instrument that rotates a plant slowly so that gravity acts equally on all sides.

sections.heading: 4. Phototropism and auxin
sections.body_md:
**How a shoot bends towards light**
1. The **tip** of the shoot senses light coming from one side.
2. **Auxin** moves to the **shaded side** and travels down the stem.
3. Cells on the shaded side **elongate more** than those on the lit side.
4. The shaded side becomes longer, so the shoot **curves towards the light**. The bending happens a short distance **below the tip**, in the zone of elongation.

**Coleoptile experiments** (oat seedlings lit from one side): an intact coleoptile bends; one with its **tip cut off** does not; one with an **opaque cap** over the tip does not; one with an **opaque collar** below the tip still bends. So the **tip perceives light** and a chemical messenger (auxin) passes down to the region that bends.

**Phototropism experiment:** grow a potted seedling in a box with an opening on one side. After a few days the shoot curves towards the opening. A control seedling lit from above grows straight.

In **roots**, auxin collecting on the lower side **slows** elongation, so the upper side grows more and the root curves downwards.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing that auxin collects on the **lit** side: it collects on the **shaded** side.
- Calling ethylene a growth promoter: it is an **inhibitor** (and a gas).
- Saying abscisic acid **opens** stomata: it **closes** them.
- Naming a tropism without **positive** or **negative**.
- Saying the tip bends: the tip **senses**; the region **below** it bends.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a hormone or tropism named, a biological term, an odd one out **with its category**.
- 2 marks: an effect with its explanation, or two uses.
- 3 marks: an experiment (set-up, observation, conclusion) or a labelled diagram of phototropism.

questions.stem_md: Leela pinches off the growing tip of her tulsi plant. Within two weeks, several side branches appear and the plant becomes bushy. Removing the tip removed the main source of

options.text_md: auxin, which had kept the side buds from growing
ethylene, which had made the side buds ripen
abscisic acid, which had made the side buds grow faster
cytokinin, which had kept the main stem short

questions.solution_md: The shoot tip makes auxin, which suppresses the lateral buds (apical dominance). Without the tip, the side buds grow — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A genetically dwarf variety of pea grows to the height of a normal pea plant when its seedlings are sprayed with
questions.solution_md: Gibberellins lengthen the internodes and overcome genetic dwarfism — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which plant growth regulator is a gas at ordinary temperatures?
questions.solution_md: Ethylene is the gaseous plant hormone — option (c).

questions.stem_md: During a long dry spell, the stomata of a maize crop stay closed for most of the day. The hormone that brings this about is
questions.solution_md: Abscisic acid, the stress hormone, closes stomata when water is short — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which hormone promotes cell division and keeps leaves green for longer by delaying their ageing?
questions.solution_md: Cytokinins promote cell division and delay senescence of leaves — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A grower sprays unpollinated tomato flowers so that the ovaries develop into fruits without seeds. The hormone sprayed is most likely
questions.solution_md: Auxins applied to flowers can make the ovary grow into a seedless (parthenocarpic) fruit — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The weedicide 2,4-D, sprayed on wheat fields to kill broad-leaved weeds, is a synthetic
questions.solution_md: 2,4-D is a synthetic auxin; in high doses it kills broad-leaved (dicot) weeds — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which pair consists only of plant growth inhibitors?
questions.solution_md: Abscisic acid and ethylene slow or stop growth processes; the other three hormones are promoters — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A cabbage plant that normally stays as a short rosette of leaves quickly forms a tall flowering stalk after one treatment. The hormone used was
questions.solution_md: Sudden elongation of the stem (bolting) in rosette plants is caused by gibberellins — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Barley grains that would not sprout were soaked in a hormone solution, and nearly all of them germinated in two days. The hormone was
questions.solution_md: Gibberellins break seed dormancy and start germination; abscisic acid does the opposite — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A trader packs a few ripe mangoes into each crate of raw mangoes. The raw ones ripen sooner because the ripe mangoes

options.text_md: give off carbon dioxide, which softens the fruit
give off ethylene gas, which hastens ripening
absorb the auxin of the raw mangoes
release abscisic acid, which sweetens the fruit

questions.solution_md: Ripe fruits release ethylene, which speeds up the ripening of nearby fruits — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Coconut water is added to the medium in which tiny pieces of plant tissue are grown in the laboratory, because it is rich in

options.text_md: cytokinins, which make the cells divide
abscisic acid, which keeps the cells dormant
auxin only, which stops all cell division

questions.solution_md: Coconut water (liquid endosperm) is a natural source of cytokinins, which promote cell division — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In autumn, a hormone builds up in the leaves of a deciduous tree, the leaves fall and the buds become dormant. This hormone is
questions.solution_md: Abscisic acid promotes leaf fall (abscission) and dormancy of buds — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Auxins, gibberellins and cytokinins are called growth promoters.

**Reason (R):** They speed up growth processes such as cell elongation and cell division.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and their effect of speeding up elongation and division is exactly why they are called promoters — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Abscisic acid is called the stress hormone of plants.

**Reason (R):** Abscisic acid makes the stomata open wider in dry weather.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The assertion is true: abscisic acid helps plants survive stress such as drought. The reason is false: it closes stomata to save water — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Ethylene is a growth promoter.

**Reason (R):** Ethylene is a plant hormone that is a gas.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The assertion is false: ethylene hastens ripening, ageing and leaf fall, so it is grouped with the inhibitors. The reason is true — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Gibberellins cause the internodes of a stem to lengthen.
questions.solution_md: True. Gibberellins make the internodes elongate, so treated plants grow taller.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Cytokinins speed up the yellowing and fall of leaves.
questions.solution_md: False. Cytokinins delay the ageing (senescence) of leaves; ethylene and abscisic acid hasten yellowing and leaf fall.

questions.stem_md: The hormone made at the shoot tip that stops the lateral buds below it from growing is ______.
questions.solution_md: Auxin.

questions.stem_md: Twenty leaves were cut from a plant and kept in the dark for six days with their stalks in a cytokinin solution; 18 of them stayed green. What percentage of these leaves stayed green?
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{18}{20} \times 100 = 90$ percent of the leaves stayed green, because cytokinin delays ageing.

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the suppression of the growth of lateral buds by the apical bud of a shoot.

answer.model_answer_md: **Apical dominance.**

questions.solution_md: Apical dominance.

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: chemical substances made in small amounts in one part of a plant that control its growth and development.

answer.model_answer_md: **Plant growth regulators** (phytohormones).

questions.solution_md: Plant growth regulators.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: Auxin, Gibberellin, Abscisic acid, Cytokinin.

answer.model_answer_md: **Abscisic acid**; the others are **growth promoters**.

questions.solution_md: Abscisic acid is a growth inhibitor.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: Fruit ripening, Leaf fall, Seed dormancy, Cell division.

answer.model_answer_md: **Cell division**; the others are **effects of growth inhibitors** (ethylene and abscisic acid).

questions.solution_md: Cell division is promoted by cytokinins.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: one ripe banana placed in a closed bag of green bananas makes them all ripen faster.

answer.model_answer_md: The ripe banana gives off **ethylene gas**, which **hastens ripening** of the green bananas.

questions.solution_md: Ethylene.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: a spray of the synthetic auxin 2,4-D can clear weeds from a wheat field without harming the wheat.

answer.model_answer_md: In high doses 2,4-D **kills broad-leaved (dicot) weeds**, but **narrow-leaved wheat (a monocot)** is not affected.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between growth promoters and growth inhibitors, giving two examples of each.

questions.stem_md: Name the three plant hormones that promote growth and state one effect of each.

questions.stem_md: Explain why abscisic acid and ethylene are grouped together, and state one effect of each that a farmer might notice.

answer.model_answer_md:

questions.passage_md: A student grew oat seedlings in the dark and then lit them from the right side only. The diagram shows four coleoptiles (young shoots) after a few hours: 1 was left intact, 2 had its tip cut off, 3 had an opaque cap over its tip, and 4 had an opaque collar round its lower part.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Coleoptiles **1 and 4**.

**(b)** Only the coleoptile **with its tip** bent; without the tip there was **no bending** and little growth. So the **tip** is needed: it produces the growth substance that causes bending.

**(c)** Covering the **tip** stopped bending, but covering the **lower part** did not. So the **tip senses the light**, and an influence passes down to the region **below the tip**, where the bending actually happens.

**(d)** It will bend to the **right**. Auxin from the tip flows down only the **left side**, so cells on the left **elongate more**; the longer left side makes the coleoptile curve away from it, even in the dark.

**(e)** The hormone is **auxin**. Apart from causing bending towards light, auxin keeps lateral buds dormant (**apical dominance**) and makes **stem cuttings form roots**; it can also produce seedless fruits.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** 1 and 4.

**(b)** Tip needed.

**(c)** Tip senses; lower region bends.

**(d)** Bends right.

**(e)** Auxin; apical dominance; rooting.

questions.stem_md: Read the following and answer the questions.
questions.passage_md: Arif sowed soaked gram seeds in a wire sieve filled with moist sawdust and hung the sieve at an angle. He kept the sawdust moist. A week later, the roots had first grown down out of the holes of the sieve and then curved back up into the sawdust.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Positive geotropism.**

**(b)** **Positive hydrotropism.**

**(c)** **Water** had the stronger effect, because the roots turned **against gravity** to reach the moist sawdust. This helps roots **find water** in the soil, even when it lies sideways or above them.

**(d)** The **shoot curves upwards**, away from gravity: it is **negatively geotropic**. The **root curves downwards**, towards gravity: it is **positively geotropic**. Auxin collects on the **lower side** of both; it makes shoot cells there grow more, but slows root cells there.

**(e)** (i) **Thigmotropism**: tendrils coil round a support they touch.
(ii) **Chemotropism**: the pollen tube grows towards the ovule.
(iii) The bending is caused by **unequal growth** (elongation) of cells on two sides of the organ, so it is **slow and permanent**, not a quick reversible movement.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Positive geotropism.

**(b)** Positive hydrotropism.

**(c)** Water stronger.

**(d)** Shoot up, root down.

**(e)** Thigmotropism; chemotropism; unequal growth.
